newsitem.title: UK: Foreign funds go cool on Korea as strikes drag on.
newsitem.headline: Foreign funds go cool on Korea as strikes drag on.

text.p: A cold wind of disillusionment has blown over foreign investors' views of South Korea, with share values dropping to decade lows and industrial strife exposing the country's deep structural problems.

South Korea held steady amid the emerging market falls of 1994 as its economy is less linked to the U.S. dollar. But since then it has greatly disappointed investors who failed to get out before the going got rough last year.
Many of its shares are at 10-year lows on valuation terms and its stock market was the second worst performer on the International Finance Corp's emerging market index last year.
Now unions say 190,000 workers are on strike over a new labour law eroding job security, and foreign funds reckon the market has further to fall.

"We are getting closer to the point where all the bad news is in the market but there could still be another wave of selling -- we haven't reached the bottom yet," said Jean De Bolle, head of strategy and global emerging market fund manager at Foreign & Colonial.

Hugh Hunter, global emerging market strategist at Barings Asset Management (BAM), agreed. "We are approaching the bottom and will probably reach it over the next month or so," he said. "Things should get better, but not in the coming quarter."
A number of foreign investors, particularly dedicated South Korea funds and long-time investors who held on to core positions, have been wrong-footed and are facing big losses.
F&C, which has $4.3 billion in emerging markets worldwide, was one of the funds that saw the writing on the wall in time.
With about four percent of its global emerging market assets invested in South Korea at the start of 1996, it began selling at mid-year and reduced its exposure to zero by the year-end.

BAM, which has about $5.5 billion invested in global emerging markets, also began cutting its exposure in South Korea at mid-year, moving to a neutral or underweight position against the main indices from overweight at the start of 1996.
But South Korea was one of the biggest contributors to F&C's performance last year. So what happened to spoil the party?

South Korea's stock market, dominated by electronics and petrochemicals, is highly cyclical and was hit by a severe downturn at mid-year. With capacity expanding all over Asia, trying to export its way out of trouble has been an uphill battle and there seems little prospect of greater demand.
"The Korean economy from a structural point of view is in deep trouble," De Bolle said.
Its major corporates, which dominate the South Korean economy, are ill-equipped for the storm.
"Companies have been encouraged to expand capacity without thinking about investment to give return on equity, and have been left in a weak position," De Bolle said.
BAM's Hunter pointed to South Korea's poor trade position, high real interest rates and lack of progress on deregulation.
Its banking system is also under stress after subsidising industry while its financial markets are crying out for reform.
The strikes against the new law making it easier to sack workers is a further sign of deep structural problems.

"Cyclically there is no sign of an upturn in Korea but even when the cycle turns, big structural problems remain," De Bolle said. "Until we see a big deregulation drive, it is difficult to see how corporate Korea will recover in a big way."
BAM's Hunter drew some hope from the presidential election, scheduled for December.
"That may prompt some sort of recovery in the second half," he said. "The government will want a feel good factor, and the situation may start to turn around looking forward."
